paragraphs.text: English translation of the verified source: “He said to them: Why do I declare impure while you declare pure, and why do I prohibit while you permit? They said to him: Because you intercalate years and establish months outside the Land of Israel. He said to them: But did Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef not intercalate years and establish months outside the Land of Israel? They replied: Leave Rabbi Akiva aside, for he left no one like himself in the Land of Israel. He said: I too left no one like myself in the Land of Israel. They replied: The kids you left have become strong goats with horns; they have sent us to you.”

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Resisei Layla 48, paragraph 3, phrases 1–8: “On the fourth day He created the sun and the moon, and in the future He will exact punishment from those who worship them. The creation of the luminaries to illuminate the world parallels the giving of the Torah, which shone the light of Torah upon all who enter the world. Our Sages of blessed memory taught (Shabbat 89b) that Mount Sinai was so named because hatred descended there upon the idolatrous nations, through the attribute of victory, the level of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, whose face was like the face of the sun (Bava Batra 75a). Our Sages of blessed memory also taught (Nedarim 8b) that in the future there will be no Gehinnom; rather, the sun will be removed from its sheath—the righteous, etc., and the wicked, etc. This follows the principle: 'The righteous shall walk in them, while sinners shall stumble in them.' Likewise, they taught (Shabbat 88b) that for those who turn to the left in Torah it becomes a potion of death; 'evil pursues sinners,' for the sin itself becomes the punishment. This is the meaning of the statement (Bava Batra 16a): he is the evil inclination; he is the Angel of Death.”

paragraphs.text: English translation of the verified source: “Noach walked with God.” Rabbi Yehudah likened this to a prince with two sons, one younger and one older: he said to the younger, “Walk with me,” but to the elder, “Come, walk before me.” Thus Avraham, whose strength was greater, was told “Walk before Me,” while Noach walked with God. Rabbi Nechemiah compared Noach to the king’s friend sinking in thick mud, whom the king summoned to walk beside him; Avraham is compared to the king’s friend who shone light for him through a window in dark alleys. The king said: “Rather than illuminating Me through a window, come illuminate before Me.” Thus the Holy One said to Avraham: “Instead of lighting My way from Mesopotamia and its cities, come and illuminate before Me in the Land of Israel.”

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Divrei Soferim 13, paragraph 1, phrase window 9–16: “… therefore one's fear of sin must precede his wisdom, as stated in Avot, for otherwise it cannot endure, and "if there is no fear, there is no wisdom." And this explains why the Talmud in Shabbat first likened it to outer keys, and then conversely likened fear to the inner courtyard and Torah to the outer gate, which appears contradictory—presenting fear as inner and Torah as the entryway—alongside the mishnaic dictum in Avot: "If there is no wisdom, there is no fear." But in truth, the fear of Hashem is itself wisdom, as stated in Devarim Rabbah [11]: "By your lives, all wisdom and the entire Torah are a single simple matter: whoever fears Me and performs words of Torah has all wisdom and the entire Torah in his heart; from where is this derived...", and this represents Lower Wisdom (Chochmah Tata'ah), the wisdom of Solomon of whom it is said, "And he was wiser than all men," which is the pinnacle of human intellect, attained in this world solely through the fear implanted in the heart. Therefore, concerning one who possesses Torah but lacks the fear of Heaven, they expounded in Yoma [72b] upon the verse "the purchase price to buy wisdom," that his Torah is merely considered currency to purchase wisdom, for the core of wisdom is the direct awareness that there is a Creator, through which awe falls upon him naturally, and from this vantage Torah is termed the entrance-gate; and thus the Sanhedrin are called "those who sit at the gate," translated in the Aramaic Targum on "to the gate" as "to the gate of the Beit Din," which serves as the gate to the courtyard and the gate unto Hashem, …”
